Skill release — the engine is byte-identical to 2.2.1; this ships the
current Standard Operating Manual to `npx ivue skill`, which installs the
copy bundled with the package.

## The Standard, extended in production

The manual grew 779 → 845 lines with conventions earned in the field
(building [Invar](https://ivue.dev/examples/invar), the 94k-line terminal
IDE on ivue):

- **Reading your own statics — the ladder.** A getter that reaches statics
  through a namespace's `Class` slot hard-binds to the base class and
  silently ignores subclass overrides (measured: a subclass setting `0.1`
  still read `0.4`). The three-rung ladder: delete the static if nothing
  outside reads it → read live off the receiver with
  `(this.constructor as typeof $X).MEMBER` → or name the class directly
  when overriding must not happen.
- **Constants get roles.** The old "plain fields for constants" guidance is
  replaced by a role table: tunable class constants are
  `static get SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE()` (overridable, receiver-followed),
  hot-path byte constants are `static readonly`, identity data is an
  instance `readonly` field, constructed dependencies come from `createX()`
  factory methods — anything else is a defect.
- **Member ordering.** One order everywhere: static members → constructor →
  state getters → prop getters → derived getters → methods.
- **Construction-order note.** Getter and prototype-method overrides
  dispatch while a parent constructor runs; subclass field initializers do
  not — which is what makes getters safe tunables and `createX()` safe
  construction seams.

  receiver-following static read in place.

- Additional `Static()` test coverage (anchor shape, composition,
  binding-order cases). Engine coverage stays 100%.
- Build tooling: `vite-plugin-dts` loads only for library builds, never
  under vitest (fixes fresh-install CI where current api-extractor releases
  break under the pinned plugin).

**Upgrade:** `npm i ivue@2.2.2`, then re-run `npx ivue skill` (or
`npx ivue skill --all`) to refresh the installed manual.

parts.text: what do you think can be built with ivue which was very hard before, what avenues does ivue (and invariants) clearly open which are intractable usually

Great question to sit with. Let me sort it by *which property does the unlocking*, because each opens a different door — and some doors are proven while others are still directional.

**1. Whole-dataset applications in the browser** — unlocked by the O(observed) cost model. The intractable thing was never rendering big data, it was *modeling* it: every mainstream reactive framework charges per-entity-that-exists (proxies, computeds, subscriptions), so a million-row model dies before the first paint, and everyone retreats to server paging and dead snapshots. ivue charges per-entity-*observed* — 20M live cells at 4.7 bytes, a million rows at O(viewport) — which means "the entire dataset *is* the client-side model, fully reactive" becomes a legitimate architecture. That's Excel-class spreadsheets, gigabyte log explorers, timeline/audio editors, genome browsers, BI tools that pivot raw data locally. This one is *proven* — the grid and scroller aren't demos, they're existence proofs.

**2. Software that's modified while it runs** — unlocked by the live class slot + identity preservation. `export let Class` plus in-place prototype transforms is the Smalltalk image made shippable: implementations swap under a running system, method edits graft onto live instances with state intact, and Invar's sealed kernel shows the disciplined version — a plugin ecosystem that folds subclasses over class slots before boot. The normally-intractable products here: deeply user-extensible apps (Excel-macro-level extensibility but with real typed classes), in-production A/B of *implementations* rather than flags, and tools that modify themselves. The JS ecosystem gave this up when state got imprisoned in component scope; ivue's objects outliving everything brings it back.

**3. Agent-operable software by construction** — unlocked by the legible object graph. This is the one I'd bet biggest on. Today, making software drivable by agents means screen-scraping (brittle) or hand-building an automation API (expensive, always lagging the UI). An ivue app's model *is* the API: `workspaceSet.active.editor.selectLine(42)` — path-addressable, no publish tax, the same graph the UI renders. Invar proves the ceiling: agents drive it, verify against it, and its test oracle is the model itself. The avenue this opens is a category: **apps born with their machine interface** — embedded copilots that read and write the exact state the user sees, RPA that doesn't break on redesigns, every app trivially an MCP server. Nobody can currently build this cheaply; here it falls out of the architecture.

**4. Reactivity as a systems discipline** — unlocked by observation-owned resources plus the pull-floor doctrine. The allocator pattern (connections, subprocesses, timers existing only while observed) generalizes to control planes: process supervisors, dev-tool daemons, home-automation and fleet dashboards where "what should be running" is *derived state* rather than imperative choreography. This is Erlang's supervision insight expressed in TypeScript with a reactive graph as the supervisor. Normally intractable because backend code has no reactivity substrate and frontend reactivity was never trusted near file descriptors — Invar's backend is the counterexample.

**5. Architecture that cannot rot — and therefore fleets that can build** — unlocked by the invariants layer more than by ivue itself. The historically intractable problem: any codebase touched by enough hands (human or agent) erodes; review vigilance doesn't scale past a certain contributor count, and "architecture" degrades into a wiki page nobody obeys. Executable contracts + AST censuses + gates turn architecture into something *enforced per merge* — which is precisely what made a thousand agent sessions additive instead of entropic. The avenue: software at contributor scales that were previously self-defeating — agent fleets as a normal construction method, regulated-domain software whose properties are continuously proven rather than annually audited, codebases designed to outlive their authors' attention.

And one honest speculative: **local-first/sync systems** might get simpler here — identity-stable plain objects sidestep the proxy-identity hell that makes CRDT merging miserable in framework-managed state — but nobody's built it yet, so that's a hypothesis, not a claim.

The compressed version: frameworks made *views* cheap; ivue makes *models* cheap — big models, long-lived models, externally-legible models. Everything above is some product category that was blocked specifically on models being expensive, mortal, or opaque. And the invariants layer is the multiplier on all five, because it's what lets those models be built by many hands — including non-human ones — without dissolving.

If you want one to chase next as a demonstration, I'd pick #3: a small "any ivue app is an MCP server" package would be a first-of-kind artifact with an obvious blog post attached — and Invar's GraphChannel is already the prior art in your own house.

# What becomes buildable

<BlogPostDate />

![What becomes buildable](/blog/what-becomes-buildable.png)

Every framework generation made *views* cheaper — faster diffing,
finer signals, less re-rendering. The model layer never got the same
gift: models stayed expensive to make big, tied to component
lifetimes, and opaque to everything outside the render loop. A lot
of software you'd like to build was never blocked on rendering. It
was blocked on models being **expensive, mortal, or opaque**.

ivue's whole design attacks exactly those three, so it's worth
naming what that opens — five categories, each unlocked by a
specific property.

## 1. Whole-dataset applications in the browser

**Unlocked by: cost proportional to what's observed.**

The intractable thing about a spreadsheet, a gigabyte log explorer,
or a genome browser was never painting it — virtual scrolling solved
that years ago. It was *modeling* it: mainstream reactivity charges
per entity that exists (a proxy here, a computed there, a
subscription each), so a million-row model collapses before first
paint, and everyone retreats to server paging and dead snapshots.

ivue charges per entity **observed**. Derivations are shared
prototype getters at zero bytes per instance; state materializes on
first touch; the [flyweight pattern](/guide/flyweight) drops per-cell
cost to [4.7 bytes across twenty million live
cells](/blog/twenty-million-cells). The consequence is an
architecture that used to be a joke: *the entire dataset is the
client-side model, fully reactive.* Excel-class spreadsheets. Log
viewers over raw gigabytes. Timeline and audio editors. BI tools
that pivot the actual data, locally. This one isn't a prediction —
the grid and the million-row scroller run on this site.

## 2. Software that's modified while it runs

**Unlocked by: the live class slot and identity-preserving
transforms.**

```ts
export let Class = Reactive($Class); // let — a live, mutable slot
```

That one keyword is the Smalltalk image made shippable: the next
call always lands in the newest version of the class, method edits
graft onto live instances with state intact, and implementations
swap under a running system. [Invar's sealed
kernel](/examples/invar) is the disciplined form — plugins fold
subclasses over class slots before boot, then the kernel freezes.

The category this reopens: **deeply extensible software**. In-app
plugin ecosystems with real typed classes instead of stringly
config. User-extensible tools at the level Excel macros hinted at.
Live A/B of *implementations*, not just flags. The JS ecosystem gave
this up when state got imprisoned inside component scope; objects
that outlive everything bring it back.

## 3. Agent-operable software, by construction

**Unlocked by: the legible object graph.**

Making software drivable by machines has always meant one of two bad
options: screen-scraping (brittle) or hand-building an automation
API that forever lags the UI (expensive). An ivue application's
model *is* the API:

```ts
workspaceSet.active.editor.selectLine(42)
```

One navigable graph — [the one the ecosystem
abandoned](/blog/the-object-graph-they-took) — path-addressable,
with no publish tax, the same state the UI renders. Invar runs on
this today: agents drive it, verify their own work against it, and
its test oracle is the model itself.

> Apps born with their machine interface. The copilot reads and
> writes the exact state the user is looking at, automation stops
> breaking on redesigns, and every app is one adapter away from
> being an MCP server.

Software that wants agents inside it — which is rapidly becoming
all software — currently pays a second-API tax to get there. Here
the interface falls out of the architecture.

## 4. Reactive control planes

**Unlocked by: observation-owned resources.**

In [Invar's backend](/blog/reactivity-is-an-allocator), database
connections, language-server processes, and timers exist only while
something observes them — reactivity working as the *allocator*,
with a pull floor underneath for correctness. Generalize that and
you get a systems discipline: process supervisors, dev-tool daemons,
home-automation and fleet dashboards where "what should be running"
is **derived state** instead of imperative choreography.

This is Erlang's supervision insight expressed in TypeScript, with
a reactive graph as the supervisor. It was intractable for a plain
reason: backend code never had a reactivity substrate, and frontend
reactivity was never trusted near file descriptors. Both halves of
that objection are now dead in one codebase.

## 5. Architecture that cannot rot

**Unlocked by: the invariants layer — contracts, censuses, gates.**

Any codebase touched by enough hands erodes. Review vigilance stops
scaling at some contributor count; "the architecture" degrades into
a wiki page nobody obeys. The discipline built around ivue turns
architecture into something *executable*: invariant contracts
stating what must hold, AST censuses counting violations, merge
gates that reject what the model contradicts —
[uniformity as a measuring instrument](/blog/uniformity-is-an-instrument),
[zeros that hold while the codebase triples](/blog/the-zeros-didnt-move).

What that opens is a contributor scale that used to be
self-defeating: agent fleets as a normal construction method, teams
where the structure carries the care instead of the reviewers,
software in regulated domains whose properties are proven
continuously rather than audited annually. This is the multiplier
on the other four — big, live, legible models are only safe to
build *by many hands* when the discipline is mechanical.

## The shape of it

One sentence version: **frameworks made views cheap; ivue makes
models cheap** — big models, long-lived models, externally legible
models — and each category above is a product family that was
blocked on exactly one of those costs. One more we suspect but
haven't proven: local-first sync should get simpler on
identity-stable plain objects, where CRDT merging never fights a
proxy for object identity — a hypothesis waiting for its builder.

The substrate is [1.1 kB](/blog/one-kilobyte-feature), the
[Standard](/guide/standard) teaches it to your team and your
agents in one document, and the proof-of-scale
[runs a full IDE](/examples/invar). Pick a door.

give me cloudflare dns config to redirect www. -> no www

Two pieces: a proxied DNS record for `www` (so Cloudflare answers for it), then a Redirect Rule that bounces it to the apex. No server involved — the redirect happens at Cloudflare's edge.

**1. DNS record** (Dashboard → ivue.dev → DNS → Records)

| Type | Name | Content | Proxy |
|---|---|---|---|
| A | `www` | `192.0.2.1` | Proxied (orange cloud) |

The IP is a dummy (192.0.2.1 is a reserved documentation address) — it's never contacted because the redirect rule fires at the edge first. The record only needs to exist and be **proxied**. `AAAA www → 100::` works too; either is fine.

**2. Redirect Rule** (Dashboard → ivue.dev → Rules → Redirect Rules → Create rule → "Single Redirect")

- **Rule name:** `www to apex`
- **When incoming requests match:** Custom filter expression
  - Field `Hostname` · Operator `equals` · Value `www.ivue.dev`
- **Then:** Dynamic redirect
  - Expression: `concat("https://ivue.dev", http.request.uri.path)`
  - Status code: **301**
  - ✅ Preserve query string

There's also a one-click template called **"Redirect from WWW to Root"** on that same Rules page — it produces exactly this rule, so you can use it instead of typing the expression.

**Verify** after saving (propagation is near-instant):

```
curl -sI https://www.ivue.dev/guide/performance | head -3
```

Expect `HTTP/2 301` with `location: https://ivue.dev/guide/performance`.

One note: since the zone is on Cloudflare, SSL for `www` is covered by the default edge certificate (`ivue.dev` + `*.ivue.dev`), so HTTPS on the www variant works without any extra cert step.

parts.text: should we use twilio or mailchimp to manage email marketing from mcp, via ai etc?

Mailchimp — and it's not close for this use case. Here's the reasoning:

**Twilio isn't really an email product.** Twilio's email arm is SendGrid, and SendGrid is at its best as an *API-first delivery pipe* — transactional mail, or marketing where you build the audience logic, templates, and compliance flow yourself. You'd be assembling list storage, double opt-in, unsubscribe handling, bounce suppression, and CAN-SPAM/GDPR footers from primitives. Great when email is a product feature; overkill for a newsletter.

**Mailchimp is the managed audience layer you'd otherwise have to build.** Signup → double opt-in → audience with consent records → unsubscribe links and suppression handled automatically → deliverability reputation managed for you. For "every blog post goes to subscribers," that's the whole job. And two things line up with what we've already built:

1. **The site is already wired for it.** `NewsletterSignup.vue` posts JSONP to a Mailchimp embedded-form action — you paste the `MAILCHIMP_ACTION` URL and the whole toast/pill/inline system goes live. Zero migration.
2. **The RSS path is the cheapest automation of all.** Once we add an RSS feed for the blog (small VitePress addition), Mailchimp's RSS campaign feature emails new posts automatically — no MCP server needed for the baseline "send every post" behavior.

**On the MCP/AI angle specifically:** both have full REST APIs, so an MCP server can drive either equally well. But what the AI would *do* differs. Against Mailchimp's Marketing API the MCP tools are high-leverage and safe: "draft a campaign from this post, subject-line variants, schedule for Tuesday 9am, report opens/clicks" — while compliance stays enforced by the platform underneath, so an agent can't accidentally send unsubscribed users mail. Against SendGrid, the agent is operating raw send infrastructure, and mistakes are spam incidents.

**When Twilio/SendGrid would win:** if ivue.dev later needs transactional mail (account emails, alerts), high-volume programmatic sends, or SMS in the same stack. That's not this.

So: create the Mailchimp account, paste the form action URL, add the RSS feed for auto-campaigns, and layer an MCP server on the Marketing API later for the editorial/AI workflows. Twilio only enters the picture if email ever becomes a runtime feature of a product rather than marketing.

i don't really want it to send an email on each new post, so the idea is if person subscribes he start receiving each blog post from the beginning of time every day or every other day, but what if we add an email that we want to send out right now, the previous line up will re-send a new email in several days, should we make it track and exclude repeats or just re-send them again later anyway?

Track and exclude — don't re-send. And the nice part is that the right data model makes deduplication free rather than a bolted-on check.

**Why not re-send anyway:** a duplicate email is the single strongest unsubscribe/spam-flag trigger a small newsletter can produce. The reader doesn't think "the drip and the broadcast overlapped" — they think "this list repeats itself," and both trust and deliverability reputation take the hit. The only legitimate re-send is a deliberate one ("this post was substantially updated"), which is an editorial decision, not a scheduler accident.

**The model that dissolves the problem:** stop thinking of the drip as a *sequence* ("day 14 → post 14") and think of it as a *per-subscriber sent-set with one rule*:

> Every send day, send the **oldest post this subscriber hasn't received**. One email per (subscriber, post), ever.

Under that rule there's no special case to handle:

- The back-catalog drip is just the rule running on someone with an empty set.
- An ad-hoc broadcast is just a send that jumps the queue — it lands in everyone's sent-set, so the drip *structurally cannot* repeat it later. No exclusion logic exists; there's nothing to exclude from.
- Frequency capping composes cleanly too: if the broadcast goes out today, it counts as today's email and the drip skips a beat, so nobody gets two in one day.

A fixed sequence, by contrast, forces you to patch every ad-hoc send with tracking — the dedup question you're asking is the symptom that "sequence" is the wrong shape.

**Practical implication for the platform choice:** this is where Mailchimp's built-in automations get tight. Mailchimp journeys are fixed sequences — "skip steps this subscriber already got via broadcast" isn't native. The workable shape is: Mailchimp stays the *audience layer* (signup, consent, unsubscribe, suppression — everything from the last answer), and the scheduling brain lives in a tiny ledger you own — a Cloudflare Worker on a daily cron with a D1/KV table of `(email, post_slug, sent_at)`, picking oldest-unsent per subscriber and sending through the Mailchimp/Mandrill API. That worker is also exactly the thing your MCP server drives later: "send this post to everyone now" is one tool call that both broadcasts and writes the ledger, so the invariant holds no matter who initiates the send — you, a cron, or an agent.

So: dedupe by construction, not by tracking-as-a-patch — and it costs you one small table.

parts.text: is cloudflare worker free?

Yes — and your use case fits comfortably inside the free tier. ivue.dev already runs on Workers, so this adds no new account or billing surface.

What the free plan includes (per day):

- **Workers**: 100,000 requests/day, 10 ms CPU per invocation. **Cron Triggers are included free** — a daily scheduled run is one invocation.
- **D1** (SQLite): 5 GB storage, 5 million rows read/day, 100,000 rows written/day.
- **KV** (if you preferred it): 100,000 reads/day, 1,000 writes/day, 1 GB.

Scale check against the newsletter ledger: one cron tick per day, and even at 10,000 subscribers a send day is ~10k ledger reads + 10k inserts + 10k outbound `fetch`es to the Mailchimp API — around 1–2% of the daily write quota and a rounding error on reads. The 10 ms CPU limit is about compute, not waiting: time spent awaiting Mailchimp's API doesn't count against it, and you'd batch the sends anyway. You would outgrow the free tier only around hundreds of thousands of subscribers, at which point the paid plan is $5/month.

The one caveat: Workers don't send email themselves — the actual delivery still goes through Mailchimp/Mandrill's API (Mandrill transactional is a paid Mailchimp add-on, which is likely your only real cost in this whole design). The Worker is just the free scheduler + ledger around it.
